content:
Holding on until the last moment

"To be honest, I held on until the last moment." Ms. Yuen's parents raised two sisters at Wang Fuk Court. After her father passed away and her elder sister got married, she lived with her mother until the great fire. Her mother perished in the blaze. During the past period of going upstairs, she once wore a sweater with the handwritten words "rebuild on the original site" to express her demands. But the authorities rejected the proposal, and the owners' corporation refused to discuss it. It was not until one week before the acquisition deadline of 31 August that she submitted her "letter accepting the acquisition offer."

Ms. Yuen believes the residents of Wang Fuk Court have been left with no way out, like a crab crushed under a boulder. She described how the two explainers she had come into contact with were unable to answer her questions, and that the only clear objective was to press neighbours for details about flat sales.

Post-disaster life is "temporary lodging"

Since the fire, she has stayed at Shan Lau in Tai Po, and later moved to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a monthly "temporary residence fee" each month. The beds, dining tables, and TV cabinets that originally existed in the unit, as well as the neighbours and security guards, all serve as constant reminders of her identity. She describes her life after the incident as "temporary lodging."

Reflecting on what "home" and "family" truly mean

Every day after work, she returns to this empty unit at eight or nine o'clock. On holidays, she chooses to leave and go to her sister's home. "Actually, since the incident, I've been thinking about what 'home' means, what 'family' means. A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when this home at Wang Fuk Court could be burned down by someone..."

"Now the word 'home' carries quite a weight for me"

When the reporter asked Ms. Yuen about her imagination of home, she said the old phone containing photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories remain only in her mind. She sighed deeply and said, "(Home) is not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, and all sorts of household appliances to make it a so-called proper home. It's made me rethink what the elements of a proper home really are, so I can't answer that question for now, because now the word 'home' carries quite a weight for me."

Dissatisfied with officials' "letting go" remarks

The responses of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire, such as Chief Secretary for Administration Deputy Cheuk Wing-hing's "letting go" theory and Financial Secretary Deputy Wong Wai-lun's talk of market value, have only added to her helplessness and indignation. "The more silent you are, the less I understand." "When they can actually say such cold-hearted things, what do they really think about the meaning of home?"

A sense of "selling at a loss"

Recalling the moment she signed the letter accepting the acquisition, Ms. Yuen said the strongest feelings were a sense of unwillingness and "bitterness," a feeling of "selling at a loss," because home is not only about real-world value but also about emotional and memory connections. "The flat was something my dad and mum worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken away for nothing, I would be even more unwilling than just 'selling at a loss' now."

After signing the letter, Ms. Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has postponed the submission of its report until October. Ms. Yuen says pursuing accountability is one part of it, "but how I personally move forward, I can't answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss. First, the home was burned down, and what that means is that it's as if the history of my growing up has been wiped away. A family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death... there's a huge hole in my heart. Can that hole really be filled? Or will there be a day when it heals? I don't know how to answer."
